title: Surface Acoustic Wave Accelerometers and Vibration Sensors: A Review of Designs, Performance, and Limitations
content: Surface acoustic wave (SAW) devices have attracted increasing interest over the past decade as a promising approach to vibration and acceleration sensing, particularly in harsh environments. Their solid state build, frequency domain output, ability to be read wirelessly and passively, and tolerance of large mechanical shocks give them practical advantages that are hard to match with suspended mass MEMS designs. This review covers the main works published in the last decade about surface acoustic wave accelerometers/vibration sensors. These papers mainly deal with: (i) sensing element architecture, from rectangular cantilevers through trapezoidal, triangular, and equal-strength beams to clamped circular membranes; (ii) substrate choice across ST-cut quartz, YX-128° lithium niobate, aluminium nitride thin films on silicon, and langasite, together with the trade-offs linking piezoelectric coupling, temperature stability, and shock survival; (iii) interdigital transducer (IDT) layout, including the non equidistant ring IDT needed on anisotropic substrates and the rectangular finger designs needed for high-Q ring resonators; (iv) wave confinement methods using phononic crystal reflectors, which, in simulation, start to separate the long standing trade-off between sensitivity and quality factor; and (v) multiphysics simulation frameworks that include the acoustoelastic effect and have become central to the design process. Reported devices now cover more than five orders of magnitude in measurement range, from sub-0.02 g detection thresholds simulated for flexible circular membranes to shock survival above 190,000 g measured in scaled lithium niobate resonators, and from room temperature to 500 °C operation in langasite based sensors with clear separation of temperature and vibration effects. A comparison table brings these results together, and the review ends by pointing out the main open problems — the gap between simulated and measured quality factors, the small amount of published data on long-term drift, and the lack of agreed reporting standards — before outlining future directions in metamaterial based confinement, integrated wireless read-out, and IC-compatible processing.
